questions.question:
Identify the concept defined below.
A conventional system of meaningful signs and rules used for communication and other mental and social activities.
questions.explanation:
A conventional system of meaningful signs and rules used for communication and other mental and social activities.
Worked example: A Deaf student in Lahore discusses a research idea using Pakistan Sign Language, while another student explains it through spoken Urdu.
Why this fits: Both use organized form-meaning relationships; sound is a modality difference rather than the defining criterion for language.
Important distinction: Natural signed languages demonstrate that language is not restricted to the vocal modality.

questions.question:
Which concept is described here?
Knowledge or use of one language, understood in relation to the definition and setting adopted.
questions.explanation:
Knowledge or use of one language, understood in relation to the definition and setting adopted.
Worked example: In a hypothetical interview, a Lahore resident reports using Urdu only but recognizes several Urdu accents.
Why this fits: Several accents within one language do not by themselves establish a repertoire of two languages.
Important distinction: Dialect diversity within a language is distinguishable from using two named languages.

questions.question:
Which term matches the following description?
Knowledge or use of two languages with potentially different abilities across tasks and settings.
questions.explanation:
Knowledge or use of two languages with potentially different abilities across tasks and settings.
Worked example: Hina discusses family routines in Punjabi and writes university assignments in English, with different strengths in each.
Why this fits: Functional use of two languages does not require identical skill in every task.
Important distinction: A functional bilingual repertoire can be uneven and change with experience.

Identify the concept defined below.
Knowledge or use of more than one language; some teaching classifications reserve the term for three or more.
questions.explanation:
Knowledge or use of more than one language; some teaching classifications reserve the term for three or more.
Worked example: A Karachi student uses Urdu, Sindhi and English in different parts of daily life.
Why this fits: Three languages fit both the broad multilingual convention and the narrower three-or-more classroom convention.
Important distinction: State the convention: broad usage includes bilingualism, while narrower classroom usage separates two from three or more.

Which concept is described here?
Knowledge or use of three languages.
questions.explanation:

Worked example: A child has meaningful opportunities to communicate in Punjabi, Urdu and English with different people.
Why this fits: The profile involves three languages; opportunities do not guarantee equal proficiency or literacy.
Important distinction: Exposure creates opportunities; proficiency depends on access, interaction and experience.

questions.question:
Identify the concept defined below.
Acquisition of two languages from infancy or very early overlapping exposure.
questions.explanation:
Acquisition of two languages from infancy or very early overlapping exposure.
Worked example: From infancy, a child has regular conversations and play in both Punjabi and Urdu with caregivers.
Why this fits: Early overlapping exposure defines the acquisition history; current dominance must be assessed separately.
Important distinction: Terminological age cutoffs vary, so describe actual exposure history rather than imposing a universal birthday boundary.

questions.question:
Which concept is described here?
Acquisition of an additional language after development in an earlier language has begun.
questions.explanation:
Acquisition of an additional language after development in an earlier language has begun.
Worked example: A Punjabi-speaking child starts regular Urdu interaction at preschool after Punjabi development has begun.
Why this fits: The additional language follows an earlier developmental start rather than beginning concurrently from infancy.
Important distinction: Successive and consecutive are commonly used for sequential acquisition; receptive ability is a different classification dimension.

Bilingual development beginning during childhood.

Why this fits: This describes a childhood start, not a guarantee of balance or future maintenance.
Important distinction: Age of onset alone does not determine proficiency, maintenance or educational conditions.

Important distinction: Receptive and expressive ability can differ because of opportunity, preference and proficiency.

A profile in which one language is stronger overall or for particular tasks.
questions.explanation:
A profile in which one language is stronger overall or for particular tasks.
Worked example: A medical student retrieves academic terms more easily in English but family expressions more easily in Urdu.
Why this fits: Dominance is task-sensitive; one overall label may hide important differences.
Important distinction: Dominance can differ by domain and change with education, migration and use.

Why this fits: Balance is relative to what was measured and cannot be generalized automatically to literacy or every topic.
Important distinction: Balance is relative to tasks and measures, not complete mastery of two entire languages.

Why this fits: The earlier language retains support while another is added; identical scores are not required.
Important distinction: Maintenance and support define the additive orientation; numerical balance is a separate issue.

concepts.definition: Knowledge or use of one language, understood in relation to the definition and setting adopted.
concepts.example: In a hypothetical interview, a Lahore resident reports using Urdu only but recognizes several Urdu accents.
concepts.false: Speaking different dialects necessarily makes a person bilingual.

concepts.comparison: Monolingualism: Knowledge or use of one language, understood in relation to the definition and setting adopted. Bilingualism: Knowledge or use of two languages with potentially different abilities across tasks and settings.

concepts.definition: Knowledge or use of two languages with potentially different abilities across tasks and settings.
concepts.example: Hina discusses family routines in Punjabi and writes university assignments in English, with different strengths in each.
concepts.false: Bilingual status requires identical scores in every skill in both languages.

concepts.definition: Knowledge or use of more than one language; some teaching classifications reserve the term for three or more.
concepts.example: A Karachi student uses Urdu, Sindhi and English in different parts of daily life.

sources.title: Baker & Wright (2021) — Foundations of Bilingual Education and Bilingualism, 7th ed.
sources.use: Recommended course book. Publisher-submitted announcement verifies authors, edition and scope. The complete copyrighted book was not accessed.

sources.title: Wardhaugh & Fuller — An Introduction to Sociolinguistics, 8th ed.
sources.use: Recommended textbook for variation, language and society. Official companion site verifies the edition; no claim of full-text review.

sources.title: Holmes & Wilson — An Introduction to Sociolinguistics, 6th ed.
sources.use: Recommended alternative textbook; publisher description checked for scope, not a substitute for access to the full book.

sources.title: Grosjean (2021) — Life as a Bilingual
sources.use: Authoritative further reading on real bilingual profiles; available publisher chapter descriptions were inspected.

sources.title: ASHA — Multilingual Service Delivery
sources.use: Professional guidance supporting the core principle that multilingualism is not a communication disorder and that service planning must consider the person’s languages.

sources.title: ASHA — Learning More Than One Language
sources.use: Accessible family guidance for multilingual development, language use and seeking support when concerns arise.

sources.title: ASHA — Cultural Responsiveness
sources.use: Professional reference for reflective practice, individualized inquiry and cultural-linguistic considerations.

sources.title: ASHA (2003) — American English Dialects
sources.use: Technical report establishing that dialect variation itself is not a pathological form of speech or language; use alongside contemporary individualized practice.

sources.title: ASHA — What Is Dynamic Assessment?
sources.use: Professional introduction to evaluating learning potential and supported performance.

sources.title: ASHA — Collaborating With Interpreters, Transliterators, and Translators
sources.use: Professional role distinctions and collaboration guidance. US-specific legal material is not presented as Pakistani law.

sources.title: Cummins (2008) — BICS and CALP: Empirical and theoretical status of the distinction
sources.use: Author’s discussion of the conversational/academic distinction; supplements the slide model without imposing rigid learning deadlines.

sources.title: Lehtonen et al. (2018) — Is bilingualism associated with enhanced executive functioning in adults?
sources.use: Meta-analytic review, Psychological Bulletin, 144(4), 394–425. DOI: 10.1037/bul0000142. Supports caution about universal cognitive-advantage claims.

sources.title: Rensch, Hallberg & O’Leary (1992) — Sociolinguistic Survey of Northern Pakistan, vol. 3: Hindko and Gujari
sources.use: Regional scholarly survey recommended for further investigation. Bibliographic record verified; the entire survey was not read. Precise regional borders and contested labels are not asserted as settled facts.

sources.title: ASHA — Communication Milestones: 19 to 24 Months
sources.use: Professional developmental guidance supporting careful correction of the slide’s rigid two-word-combination timeline; milestones inform review rather than replace individual assessment.

sources.title: NBME — Item-Writing Guide
sources.use: General item-writing principles informed review of focused one-best-answer cases. These original practice items are not official, endorsed or psychometrically validated NBME questions.
